messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Luca had always been a dancer at heart. For decades, he had twirled across stages, entertaining crowds with his energetic performances. But one fateful evening, while rushing to a show, Luca's car struck a pedestrian, leaving the young woman with severe injuries. The accident shook him to his core, and the once-carefree dancer began to unravel. As time passed, certain triggers started to haunt Luca. Whenever he heard songs that had been playing on the radio during the drive, he felt an overwhelming sense of dread wash over him. The catchy tunes now served as a cruel reminder of that terrible night, transporting him back to the scene of the accident. Similarly, crowded spaces began to unnerve him; the thought of being surrounded by people made his mind wander to the chaos and panic that followed the crash. Luca couldn't shake off the memory of the accident, replaying it in his head like a gruesome loop. He dwelled on how he used to be before the event – carefree, confident, and full of life. He missed those days, but they seemed irretrievable now. To cope with these painful memories, Luca started avoiding places that reminded him of the accident, steering clear of streets where it had happened. He even suppressed thoughts about the trauma, pushing them deep into his mind in a desperate attempt to silence the guilt and self-blame. However, these maladaptive strategies only seemed to fuel his distress. The weight of his perceived failure as a protector – he should have done more to prevent the accident – continued to haunt him. He couldn't forgive himself for not being able to save the young woman from harm, and this inaction guilt gnawed at his conscience day and night. Luca felt like he had failed in his most important role in life: as a guardian of others' safety. As these negative appraisals took hold, they began to shape his perception of the world around him. He started to notice cars hitting each other by accident – or even just slowing down at intersections – and would immediately think of that fateful night. These flashbacks left Luca on edge, always ready for disaster to strike again. His concentration waned, making it difficult to focus on anything else. Even when he knew he was in a safe place, his body remained tense, as if anticipating the next catastrophe. The resulting hypervigilance began to disrupt his life, especially at night. Luca found himself lying awake for hours, too alert to relax and fall asleep. His exhaustion only exacerbated the anxiety that had taken up residence within him. Certain triggers – those songs, crowded spaces – now seemed even more menacing than before, feeding into the cycle of fear and self-doubt. In his line of work as a dancer, these symptoms were becoming increasingly debilitating. Luca's usual performances were marred by mistakes and missed cues, as if his brain was stuck in an endless loop of threat monitoring. The lack of control over his thoughts and emotions terrified him – what would happen to his career? To his relationships? It was only when his wife expressed her concern about the strain on their relationship that Luca realized he needed help. He couldn't bear the thought of losing everything he held dear due to this all-consuming anxiety. As he sat in the therapist's office, he hoped for one thing: to find a way out of this suffocating cycle and rediscover his passion for life – or at least learn to forgive himself enough to live with it.
